Five verbs. Almost every table you will ever need is some arrangement of these.

| Verb | Does what | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| `filter()` | keeps rows that match a condition | fewer rows |
| `select()` | keeps columns you name | fewer columns |
| `mutate()` | adds or changes a column | more columns |
| `group_by()` | splits into groups | nothing visible |
| `summarise()` | collapses each group to one row | far fewer rows |

## The dataset

We use one small cohort throughout this page. Twelve people, followed up for a
cardiovascular event.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Run the cells from the top.** The first one builds the data that all the
others use. If a later cell says `object not found`, you have skipped it.
:::


```{webr}
library(dplyr)

cohort <- tibble(
  id        = sprintf("P%02d", 1:12),
  district  = c("Kolar","Kolar","Kolar","Tumkur","Tumkur","Tumkur",
                "Hassan","Hassan","Hassan","Kolar","Tumkur","Hassan"),
  sex       = c("F","M","F","M","F","M","F","M","F","M","F","M"),
  age       = c(34, 51, 62, 45, 38, 71, 29, 55, 48, 66, 41, 59),
  smoker    = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE,
                FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE),
  years_fu  = c(5.0, 4.2, 5.0, 3.1, 5.0, 2.4, 5.0, 4.8, 5.0, 1.9, 5.0, 3.6),
  event     = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE,
                FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)
)

cohort
```

`years_fu` is how long each person was followed. It is shorter for some people,
because they had the event or were lost to follow-up.

Add those years up and you have **person-time**: the total time the group was
actually watched. It is what you divide by when people were followed for
different lengths. Primer 6 is about that.

## `filter()`: keep rows

The condition goes inside. Note **`==`**, two equals signs, for "is equal to".
One equals sign is assignment and will not work here.

```{webr}
cohort |> filter(district == "Kolar")
```

Several conditions, separated by commas, means **and**:

```{webr}
cohort |> filter(smoker, age >= 50)
```

`smoker` on its own works because it is already `TRUE`/`FALSE`. Writing
`smoker == TRUE` is the same thing, more typing.

For **or**, use `|`.

For "is it one of these", use `%in%`. It reads better than 3 `|`s in a row:

```{webr}
cohort |> filter(district %in% c("Kolar", "Hassan"))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `filter()` drops `NA` rows without telling you
If `age` is missing for someone, `age >= 50` is `NA`, not `TRUE`. That row
disappears from `filter(age >= 50)` **and** from `filter(age < 50)`.

Your 2 groups then do not add up to your total, and nothing warns you. Count
your rows before and after every filter.
:::

## `select()`: keep columns

```{webr}
cohort |> select(id, age, event)

# A minus sign drops instead
cohort |> select(-sex, -years_fu)
```

## `mutate()`: add a column

The new column is computed from existing ones, for every row at once.

```{webr}
cohort |>
  mutate(age_group = if_else(age >= 50, "50+", "under 50")) |>
  select(id, age, age_group)
```

`if_else()` takes three things: the test, what to use when it is true, what to
use when it is false. For more than two categories, `case_when()` does the same
job with as many branches as you like:

```{webr}
cohort |>
  mutate(age_band = case_when(
    age < 40            ~ "under 40",
    age < 60            ~ "40-59",
    .default            = "60+"
  )) |>
  select(id, age, age_band)
```

Read each line as "if this, then that". The first matching line wins, so order
matters: a 35-year-old is caught by the first line and never reaches the second.

## `group_by()` and `summarise()`: the pair that does the work

`group_by()` looks like it does nothing. `summarise()` then collapses each group
to a single row.

```{webr}
cohort |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_age  = round(mean(age), 1),
    events    = sum(event),
    risk      = round(mean(event), 3)
  )
```

Look at `risk`. `event` is `TRUE`/`FALSE`, so `sum()` counts the events and
`mean()` gives the proportion who had one.

That proportion is the **risk** in each district. That is a stratified
analysis, in 4 lines.

`n()` counts rows in the group and takes no arguments. Put it in every
`summarise()` you write.

A mean over 3 people and a mean over 300 look identical on the page. The
denominator is the only thing that tells them apart.

## Putting it together

```{webr}
cohort |>
  filter(age >= 40) |>
  group_by(smoker) |>
  summarise(
    n      = n(),
    events = sum(event),
    risk   = round(mean(event), 3)
  )
```

Two risks: one for smokers, one for non-smokers, among people aged 40 and over.
Divide one by the other and you have a risk ratio. That is Primer 7.

## What you should now be able to do

- Keep rows with `filter()`, and remember that `NA` rows vanish from both sides.
- Keep or drop columns with `select()`.
- Add a computed column with `mutate()`, using `if_else()` or `case_when()`.
- Produce a grouped table with `group_by()` and `summarise()`, always including
  `n()`.
- Get a risk from `mean()` of a logical column, and a rate by dividing by
  person-time instead.
